articles.headline: Agents struggle with the same bad UX we do
articles.blurb: Computer-use AI agents frequently fail at the same confusing interfaces that frustrate humans, including ambiguous buttons, hidden menus, unexplained disabled states, and disruptive overlays. People often compensate for these problems by guessing, backtracking, or relying on experience, while agents expose the underlying design debt through repeatable failures that are easier to observe. Making interfaces clearer for agents through explicit labels, visible states, predictable interactions, and semantic structure can also improve accessibility and usability for people.

articles.headline: Everyone is building AI agents. Who's designing the stop button?
articles.blurb: AI agents introduce unpredictable behavior into products traditionally designed around explicit rules and known transitions, making it essential to distinguish where autonomy is useful from where reliability is mandatory. Products can let AI interpret intentions and construct workflows while using deterministic execution, visible uncertainty, confirmation steps, and clear recovery mechanisms to protect consequential actions. Designing effective agent experiences increasingly means defining boundaries around what AI may decide, when humans must intervene, and how users can understand, correct, or stop an autonomous process.

articles.headline: Why 10,000 experiments work better than 10,000 hours for designers

Instead of relying on experience alone, designers can break career goals into microskills and run small experiments, such as opening every design review with a specific decision or presenting research findings themselves. A weekly reflection can help turn these experiments into deliberate professional growth without requiring organizational approval or major changes to existing workflows.

Its 28 styles represent different tokenizers from OpenAI, Meta, Google, DeepSeek, and others, combining contextual glyph substitutions with built-in color palettes to approximate token boundaries. Most styles achieve roughly 98% agreement with real tokenizers in testing, demonstrating how advanced font technology can perform surprisingly complex text processing while revealing its limitations around line breaks, uncommon words, and tokenization algorithms.

Shopify's Shop Pay is among the first live deployments. Mastercard is betting on network tokens over one-time virtual card numbers as the core primitive. Visa, Stripe, and PayPal are building parallel infrastructure. Holiday shopping is expected to be the first high-volume stress test for agentic payment rails at scale.

articles.headline: SEC Token Taxonomy FAQ Clarifies Decentralization Standards for Builders
articles.blurb: The SEC released a new FAQ expanding its token taxonomy framework, drawing on three clarifications flagged by a16z crypto General Counsel Miles Jennings. Q 1.4 confirms that projects can maintain decentralized governance while using legal entities like DUNAs (Decentralized Unincorporated Nonprofit Associations), resolving a structural question teams have faced when adding off-chain legal wrappers to on-chain protocols. Q 1.5 draws a formal line between permissioned and permissionless systems, and Q 1.6 separates "functional" tokens from tokens that qualify as investment contracts under securities law. Builders now have clearer criteria from the SEC to determine whether their protocol architecture and token design fall outside the agency's jurisdiction.

articles.headline: Crypto Protocols Are Winning the AI Inference Price War
articles.blurb: Centralized inference providers face structural pricing floors tied to manual approval gates, regional electricity costs, and capital-market margin requirements, creating an opening for permissionless crypto routing layers. Surplus lets holders of excess API credits from OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek sell at a discount for USDC with no KYC, posting 57x token growth (10B to 570B tokens/day) and 78x request growth (143k to 11.2M/day) over the past 90 days. Engy runs a global miner competition on hardware and electricity efficiency, growing from 2.7B to 153B tokens/day while buyback-directed revenue climbed from $363 to $8,000/day in the same window. With the inference market at $160B/year and projected to reach $350B, autonomous AI agents consuming 5x more tokens than humans will concentrate purchasing power in the cheapest available providers, positioning these protocols to capture a growing share of AI compute spend as agent usage scales.

articles.headline: Agentic commerce overhyped today; underhyped for the next 3-6 months
articles.blurb: Agentic commerce is overhyped on current usage but will be underhyped on volume within 3-6 months, and products not optimized for agents will be left behind. Most consumers outside SF don't use agents at all, and current products mainly serve high-income, tech-forward users. articles.headline: 'Leaders all over the world understand that Trump is only there for two more years & then he's gone'
articles.blurb: In American politics, the possession of presidential power does not necessarily guarantee the capacity to exercise it. Few contemporary leaders have embodied this contradiction as dramatically as Donald Trump. Following what political scientist Ian Bremmer describes as the most consequential electoral reversal for a governing party in more than half a century, the founder of Eurasia Group and GZERO Media argues that the United States has entered a new political phase: the beginning of the end of Trump's capacity to dominate the domestic and international agenda. In this wide-ranging interview with France 24, Bremmer revisits his provocative thesis that America has already reached "peak Trump." Far from suggesting that the president has become powerless, he contends that his authority is increasingly constrained by congressional opposition, Republican discontent, unpopular foreign policy decisions and the growing awareness among international leaders that the present administration has a limited political horizon. The historical reversal is, in Bremmer's account, extraordinary: "Trump back in 2024 engineered for himself the biggest political comeback in American political history. And now, only two years later, the biggest loss in 50 years." At the heart of his analysis lies a fundamental distinction between institutional authority and political influence. Trump remains commander-in-chief, retains the instruments of executive government and continues to command extraordinary media attention. Yet Bremmer argues that the president's ability to translate those advantages into effective political outcomes is diminishing. The consequences, he suggests, extend far beyond Washington. From the war in Iran and the unresolved conflict in Ukraine to the future of transatlantic relations, America's allies and adversaries are beginning to adjust their strategic calculations to a post-Trump political landscape. As Bremmer puts it: "Those foreign leaders will start to engage more with the America that they expect to deal with after Trump is gone." Equally significant is his diagnosis of the domestic forces driving this transformation. Economic disillusionment, unfulfilled electoral promises and accusations of political self-interest have, in his assessment, undermined the very coalition that propelled Trump back to the White House. Meanwhile, the president's apparent preoccupation with monumental projects and personal legacy raises a deeper question about the relationship between political spectacle and the responsibilities of governance. Bremmer's conclusion is unambiguous: "Yes, two more years to go. But nowhere near the level of disruption that he had on the global stage at the beginning of this term." The interview ultimately raises a question of profound significance for American democracy and the international order: Can a president retain the formal powers of the world's most consequential political office while progressively losing the political authority necessary to shape its future? Bremmer believes that process is already underway.
